name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH16_DIAGRAM_Q01 - Anatomical regions of human stomach

questiontext.text: Refer to the schematic diagram of the human stomach below. Identify the anatomical regions labelled P, Q, R, and S.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The schematic diagram illustrates a J-shaped human stomach receiving the oesophagus superiorly and opening into the duodenum distally, with four internal regions labelled P, Q, R, and S.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Standard anatomical orientation is used: superior is toward the top of the diagram, and the gastro-oesophageal junction lies near the upper curvature while the pyloric sphincter leads to the duodenum on the lower left.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The human stomach, located in the upper left portion of the abdominal cavity, has four major anatomical parts: the cardiac portion (where the oesophagus opens), the fundic region (the upper dome-shaped region), the body (the main central region), and the pyloric portion (which opens into the first part of the small intestine, the duodenum).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Region P lies at the superior dome-shaped bulge above the oesophageal opening, so P is the fundic region (fundus). Region Q is located immediately where the oesophagus opens into the stomach, so Q is the cardiac portion. Region R occupies the large main central part of the stomach, so R is the body. Region S is the distal narrowed portion leading toward the duodenum, so S is the pyloric portion.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking the anatomical sequence from the oesophageal entry and superior dome down to the duodenal exit confirms the assignments: P is Fundus, Q is Cardiac, R is Body, and S is Pyloric.

answer.text: P – Cardiac, Q – Fundus, R – Body, S – Pyloric
P – Fundus, Q – Cardiac, R – Body, S – Pyloric
P – Fundus, Q – Body, R – Cardiac, S – Pyloric
P – Pyloric, Q – Cardiac, R – Body, S – Fundus

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH16_DIAGRAM_Q02 - Histology of transverse section of gut

questiontext.text: The schematic diagram below represents the transverse section of the human alimentary canal. Which labelled layer is formed of loose connective tissues containing nerves, blood, and lymph vessels, and also houses glands in the duodenum?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The transverse section of the alimentary canal shows a central lumen surrounded by four concentric histological layers labelled from outermost to innermost as W, X, Y, and Z.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
From the outer peritoneal surface inward toward the lumen, the wall of the alimentary canal from oesophagus to rectum consists of four basic layers in fixed sequence.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The four layers from outside to inside are: (1) Serosa (outermost thin mesothelium with connective tissues), (2) Muscularis (smooth muscles arranged in inner circular and outer longitudinal layers), (3) Sub-mucosa (loose connective tissues containing nerves, blood and lymph vessels, and Brunner's glands in the duodenum), and (4) Mucosa (innermost layer lining the lumen).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Matching the concentric layers from outside to inside: W is the outermost layer (serosa), X is the double-layered smooth muscle coat (muscularis), Y is the third layer lying between muscularis and mucosa (sub-mucosa), and Z is the innermost layer lining the lumen (mucosa). Therefore, the layer containing loose connective tissues, nerves, blood and lymph vessels, and duodenal glands is layer Y.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Counting from the lumen outward confirms that the innermost layer is Z (mucosa) and the layer immediately external to it is Y (sub-mucosa). Thus, the correct layer is Layer Y.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH16_DIAGRAM_Q03 - Duct system of liver, gall bladder and pancreas

questiontext.text: In the schematic diagram of the duct systems of the liver, gall bladder, and pancreas below, identify the duct labelled 3 (formed by the union of ducts 1 and 2) and name the sphincter that guards the opening of duct 5 into the duodenum.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The schematic shows the gall bladder, hepatic ducts from the liver, the pancreas, and the C-shaped duodenum, with five ductal segments numbered 1 through 5.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Bile flows from the hepatic cells via hepatic ducts and from the gall bladder via the cystic duct, uniting before joining the pancreatic duct to enter the duodenum.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The duct of the gall bladder (cystic duct) joins the common hepatic duct from the liver to form the common bile duct. The common bile duct and the pancreatic duct then open together into the duodenum as the common hepato-pancreatic duct, which is guarded by the sphincter of Oddi.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
In the diagram, 1 is the cystic duct from the gall bladder and 2 is the common hepatic duct formed by the ducts from the liver. Their union forms duct 3, which is the common bile duct. Duct 3 then joins duct 4 (the pancreatic duct) to form duct 5 (the common hepato-pancreatic duct), whose opening into the duodenum is guarded by the sphincter of Oddi.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The gastro-oesophageal sphincter regulates the oesophagus-stomach junction and the pyloric sphincter guards the stomach-duodenum opening, whereas the hepato-pancreatic duct opening is guarded by the sphincter of Oddi. Hence, duct 3 is the common bile duct and the sphincter is the sphincter of Oddi.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH16_DIAGRAM_Q04 - Intestinal villi structure and fat absorption

questiontext.text: The schematic diagram below shows a section of small intestinal mucosa with villi. Identify the central vessel labelled M and state the form in which digested fats are transported into it from the intestinal mucosa.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram depicts finger-like projections (villi) of the small intestinal mucosa containing a central yellow vessel (M) surrounded by a vascular capillary network (N), with a tubular invagination (O) at the base between adjacent villi.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In each intestinal villus, blood capillaries lie peripherally beneath the epithelial lining while a single large central lymph vessel runs along the core of the villus.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Villi are supplied with a network of capillaries and a large central lymph vessel called the lacteal. Because fatty acids and glycerol are insoluble, they cannot be absorbed directly into the blood. They are first incorporated into micelles to enter the intestinal mucosa, where they are re-formed into very small protein-coated fat globules called chylomicrons and transported into the lacteals.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Structure M occupies the central axis of the villus, identifying it as the lacteal (whereas N represents the capillary network and O represents a crypt of Lieberkuhn). Digested fats (fatty acids and glycerol) enter the mucosal cells as micelles and are packaged inside the mucosa into protein-coated fat globules called chylomicrons before being transported into the lacteal (M).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Micelles are the form in which fatty acids and glycerol enter the mucosal epithelial cells from the intestinal lumen, whereas chylomicrons are the protein-coated globules transported from the mucosa into the lacteal. Thus, M is the lacteal, and digested fats are transported into it as chylomicrons.

answer.text: Crypt of Lieberkuhn; Fatty acids and glycerol
